definition.text: An economy that absorbs as much greenhouse gas as it emits, or more broadly one whose activities produce far lower emissions.

facts.text: Similar terms include green economy, carbon-neutral economy and decarbonised economy; 'carbon' stands for all greenhouse gases.
Getting there means cutting emissions in every sector, through renewables, efficiency, electric vehicles, heat pumps and climate-smart agriculture.
It needs energy policies and financial incentives such as emissions trading and carbon taxes.
Besides mitigation it brings benefits for ecosystems, trade, jobs, health, energy security and competitiveness.
Workers in carbon-intensive industries are more likely to lose jobs, while new jobs come from renewables and building renovation.
Switching to lower-emission technologies often pays back within 0.5–5 years.
Climate change is often framed as a free-rider problem: each country gains from others' mitigation but loses by going low-carbon alone.

definition.text: Electricity produced with far lower lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions than fossil fuel power.

facts.text: Sources include wind, solar, nuclear and most hydropower; fossil plants count only when fitted with carbon capture.
Almost 40% of global electricity came from low-carbon sources in 2020: about 10% nuclear, almost 10% wind and solar, and around 20% hydro and other renewables.
Very little comes from fossil sources, mostly because carbon capture is costly.
Moving to low-carbon power is among the most important actions to limit climate change.

title: Nuclear power in decarbonisation

definition.text: The disagreement over whether expanding nuclear power is needed to reach a low-carbon economy.

facts.text: The IEA, the IAEA and the UN Economic Commission for Europe hold that decarbonisation is not possible without some nuclear expansion.
Nuclear is low-carbon but carries risks and rising costs.
Environmental and security risks could outweigh its benefits.

contested_note: Agencies see nuclear expansion as necessary, while others stress its risks and costs.

title: Solar radiation modification

definition.text: Large-scale methods to limit global warming by reflecting more sunlight away from Earth back to space; also called solar geoengineering.

facts.text: It is meant to complement, not replace, cuts in greenhouse gas emissions.
Models consistently show it could reduce warming and many climate effects, but effects would vary by region and season.
It is the only known way to lower global temperatures within months.
Direct costs could be billions to tens of billions of US dollars per degree Celsius of cooling, low compared with climate damages.
It does not lower CO2, so it does nothing about ocean acidification.
Some fear it would weaken the will to cut emissions, a 'moral hazard' whose size experts dispute.
Low cost and feasibility mean one country could deploy it alone, and no comprehensive global framework regulates it.

contested_note: Scientists, NGOs and governments disagree on whether SRM should be researched or deployed at all.

definition.text: Putting small reflective particles into the upper atmosphere to reflect sunlight and cool the planet.

facts.text: It is the most-researched SRM method; the IPCC found high agreement it could limit warming to below 1.5 °C.
Sulfates are the usual proposal because volcanic eruptions release them naturally.
A key risk is delaying the recovery of the ozone layer.

definition.text: Spraying tiny sea-water droplets into low ocean clouds to make them reflect more sunlight.

facts.text: Its cooling would be felt quickly and could be reversed on fairly short time scales.
Technical barriers remain, it could not offset all current warming, and its risks are unclear.

definition.text: The rapid warming that would follow if solar radiation modification masking much warming were stopped suddenly.

facts.text: Abrupt termination with high greenhouse gas levels would bring fast temperature rise, sea level rise and weaker carbon sinks.
Large-scale SRM would likely need a commitment of decades to a century.
The IPCC notes a gradual phase-out with mitigation would reduce the impact.
